track.label: Executive Communication & Storytelling
track.summary: Develop the communication skills that define senior leaders — structured thinking with the Pyramid Principle, data storytelling, high-stakes presentation delivery, and concise written communication for C-suite audiences.
track.name: exec-communication

phases.title: Executive Presence Fundamentals
phases.description: Understand what executive presence really means — how voice, body language, pacing, and gravitas shape how others perceive and listen to you.

phases.title: Structured Communication
phases.description: Apply the Pyramid Principle and SCQA framework to structure every communication — emails, memos, and verbal briefings — so your audience gets your answer first.

phases.title: Presentation & Slide Design
phases.description: Design slides that support your narrative rather than replace it — mastering visual hierarchy, slide architecture, and the principles behind consultant-grade decks.

phases.title: Storytelling with Data
phases.description: Turn numbers into decisions by choosing the right chart, eliminating noise, and building a narrative arc that moves executives from insight to action.

phases.title: High-Stakes Speaking
phases.description: Prepare for your most important communication moments — board presentations, C-suite briefings, handling hostile questions, and leading in a crisis.

phases.title: Written Communication & Memos
phases.description: Write the memos and emails that get read — concise, direct, and structured for busy senior readers who skim first and dig in only if warranted.

topics.title: Defining Executive Presence
topics.description: Break down what executive presence actually is — the three components of gravitas, communication, and appearance — and learn how to audit your own strengths and gaps.

steps.d: Identify where you fall short in gravitas, communication, or appearance by rating yourself 1-10 on each and noting which one holds you back most in meetings.

steps.t: Record yourself speaking for one minute
steps.d: Set up your phone camera and record a brief thought without notes, then watch it back to spot the vocal and body language habits you need to change.
Observe three people you respect in meetings and write down the specific things they do with voice, posture, and pacing that command attention.
Choose one behavior from the three dimensions—a pause pattern, a posture shift, or an eye-contact technique—and commit to practicing it in your next three meetings.
After applying your chosen behavior for one week, ask a colleague if they notice any difference in how you show up, and note their specific observation.

topics.title: Vocal Delivery and Body Language
topics.description: Develop the physical signals of confidence: controlled pace, intentional pausing, open posture, and eye contact patterns that hold attention in meetings and presentations.

steps.d: Record yourself on a call or presentation and note your pace (words per minute), pause frequency, and any filler words or upspeak.
Record a two-minute explanation of your current project, then re-record it 20% slower with deliberate pauses before key points.

steps.t: Study body language in a mirror
steps.d: Stand as you normally do, then adopt an open posture with shoulders back and arms visible, and hold it for one minute while noting how differently you feel.

steps.t: Map eye contact patterns in meetings
steps.d: In your next meeting, practice looking at one person per sentence instead of scanning, and count how many people you make genuine contact with.
Create a one-minute video pitching an idea using your improved pace, pauses, posture and eye-contact discipline, then review it against a slow-paced reference.

topics.title: Commanding Attention in Any Room
topics.description: Learn frameworks for opening strong, reading the room, and recapturing attention — skills that separate communicators who are merely clear from those who are compelling.

steps.d: Draft opening lines for three different contexts (team update, C-suite brief, crisis moment) that create immediate attention without a question or story.
In your next meeting before speaking, scan for energy level, device usage, and body language, then adjust your opening intensity to match what you see.
Deliver a one-minute update, then pause for exactly five seconds of silence, watching how people re-engage and lean in.
When you sense attention flagging in a meeting, use a specific phrase like "Here's the critical piece" or "Watch this" plus a pause to reset focus.
Record a meeting you led, then watch it back and mark every moment you lost or regained room attention, identifying your personal patterns.

topics.title: The Pyramid Principle: Answer First
topics.description: Master Barbara Minto's Pyramid Principle — the standard for executive communication at McKinsey and other top firms — and practise structuring ideas from the top down.

steps.t: Build a pyramid for one decision
steps.d: Take a business decision you've recently made and write it using the Pyramid structure: governing thought on top, three supporting arguments, evidence under each.

steps.t: Convert a rambling thought to pyramid
steps.d: Take a two-minute explanation of a recent project problem and rewrite it as a pyramid, leading with your answer and stripping everything else.

steps.t: Present your pyramid to a colleague
steps.d: Deliver a two-minute verbal pyramid to someone unfamiliar with the topic and ask them to tell you the answer without your explanation.
Find an email or memo you wrote this week, identify your main point, and rewrite it leading with that point instead of building to it.
Write a one-page recommendation to a peer or manager using pyramid structure and ask them to confirm they got your core recommendation without re-reading.

topics.title: The SCQA Framework
topics.description: Use the Situation-Complication-Question-Answer framework to open emails, memos, and verbal briefings in a way that immediately engages busy decision-makers.

steps.d: Take three recent emails or updates you've written and mark where you bury the question and answer—how far down does your reader get?
Take one pressing issue at work and structure it as Situation (one sentence), Complication (one sentence), Question (one sentence), Answer (one sentence).
Take a rambling email you received or wrote and restructure it using SCQA, placing the answer up top.
Start your next team meeting with a one-minute SCQA setup for a decision or update, then deliver just that first.

steps.t: Compare your opening vs their opening
steps.d: After using SCQA in two meetings, ask attendees if getting the answer first changed how they listened, and write down their response.

topics.title: Writing Clear Recommendations
topics.description: Structure persuasive written recommendations — leading with your conclusion, supporting with grouped arguments, and anticipating the objections your reader will raise.

steps.d: Write a one-paragraph recommendation on a real topic, then write three objections below it that you anticipate.
Rewrite the recommendation so each anticipated objection is answered before it's raised, grouping your supporting arguments by theme.

steps.t: Grade your structure against the brief
steps.d: Write a short recommendation memo on a decision, read it from your reader's perspective, and mark where you lose them or where they'd want more proof.

steps.t: Test on a peer or manager
steps.d: Share your recommendation with a peer and ask what would make them say yes, and whether they had any lingering doubts after reading it.
Revise your recommendation to address their doubts, then re-share it and confirm that it's now more persuasive.

topics.title: Slide Structure and Narrative Arc
topics.description: Learn the difference between a document and a presentation deck, and apply the storyboard approach used by McKinsey, BCG, and Duarte to structure slide narratives.

steps.d: Take one message or decision you need to communicate and write it as a story: what is (current state), what changes, what's at stake, what's the new state you're proposing.
Create 6-8 slide titles (not content) that move your audience from what they know to what you want them to believe.
Sketch out or outline a five-slide narrative that answers: why this matters, what's the problem, why current solutions don't work, your recommendation, next steps.
Draft a one-page memo and a three-slide deck on the same topic and notice how the deck forces you to cut ruthlessly while the memo can be thorough.
Deliver your five-slide deck out loud to a colleague and time it—it should take 3-5 minutes—then ask if they understand your recommendation without you explaining.

topics.title: Visual Design Principles for Executive Decks
topics.description: Apply the core visual design principles — contrast, alignment, proximity, whitespace — to create slides that guide the eye and make one point per slide.

steps.t: Audit a good deck for principles
steps.d: Find a consultant deck or presentation you admire and mark every slide for contrast (color/size), alignment (grid), proximity (grouping), and whitespace.
Take a text-heavy slide and redeploy the content using contrast (bold key words), alignment (flush left or centered), proximity (group related items), and breathing room.
Review a draft deck and rewrite titles to be claims, not topic headers—"30% of users abandon without onboarding" instead of "User onboarding."
Build a five-slide deck where the largest type is reserved for the one insight per slide, supporting numbers are half that size, and details are smallest.
Redesign one cluttered slide following design principles and present both versions to a peer, asking which one delivers the message faster.

topics.title: Slide Makeovers and Common Mistakes
topics.description: Practise diagnosing and fixing the most common slide failures: text-heavy builds, unclear charts, weak titles, and mismatched story and visuals.

steps.t: Find a cluttered slide to fix
steps.d: Identify a real slide from your recent work or from online that's text-heavy, has too many colors, or has weak visual hierarchy.
List what's wrong with the slide: too much text, unclear hierarchy, competing colors, unclear title, missing data source?
Redesign the slide making only one major change per iteration (cut half the text, then fix hierarchy, then simplify colors) and note how much clearer it becomes.
Show a colleague the before-and-after and ask what insight now jumps out—if they immediately see your point, the makeover worked.

steps.t: Fix one more slide from your deck
steps.d: Apply the same process to a second weak slide in your deck and confirm it's now clearer and faster to understand.

topics.title: Choosing the Right Chart Type
topics.description: Use the chart chooser framework to match your data relationship — comparison, composition, distribution, relationship — to the chart that communicates it most clearly.

steps.d: Take five datasets from your work and name what relationship each shows: comparison (which is bigger), composition (what parts), distribution (how spread), or relationship (what moves together).
For each of those five datasets, select the chart type that best communicates that relationship and explain why in one sentence.
Take one dataset and sketch three different chart types for it (bar, line, pie), then decide which one tells the story your audience needs to hear.
Audit a real presentation you're building and remove any chart that takes more than five seconds to understand or that doesn't directly support a claim.
Design one chart for your next presentation that shows a comparison or relationship clearly, then test it by showing it to a colleague with no explanation.

topics.title: Decluttering and Emphasising Data
topics.description: Apply Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic's principles: remove chart junk, use pre-attentive attributes strategically, and direct your reader's attention to exactly the insight you need them to see.

steps.d: Find one of your charts or a published chart with a lot of detail and list every element: gridlines, legends, multiple colors, data labels, axis labels.
Redraw or edit that chart removing every element that doesn't serve your insight—usually half the chart elements can go.
Highlight the one data point or series that proves your argument using color or size, making that element pop before any reading.
Show your cleaned-up chart to someone for three seconds, then ask what they see first—if it's not your insight, your pre-attentive design failed.
Apply the decluttering principles to a new chart in your current work and measure the before-and-after clarity with a colleague.

topics.title: From Numbers to Narrative
topics.description: Build a complete data story: context, conflict, resolution — transforming a set of charts into a coherent argument that moves executives toward a decision.

steps.d: Take a dataset and map a narrative arc: what's the opening insight, what do we not yet know, what complication emerges, what's the resolution?
Create 3-5 charts that move your audience through context, conflict, and resolution around a single business question.
String your three-act chart sequence together with one-sentence transitions that explain how each chart builds on the last.

steps.t: Test the story arc with an audience
steps.d: Present your chart sequence to a peer or team as a story and ask if they felt the arc and what decision it led them toward.
Based on feedback, adjust which charts you use, their order, or the transitions to make the story more compelling or clear.

topics.title: Presenting to Board and C-Suite Audiences
topics.description: Adapt your content, structure, and pacing for the most senior audiences — who read ahead, interrupt often, and need you to lead with implications, not context.

steps.d: For your next board or C-suite presentation, list what the three most senior people in the room want to know, and what they don't care about.
Remove all background, process, and detail from your presentation, keeping only implications and decisions.
Restructure your deck so the first thing you say is what the audience should do or decide, not the context.
Write down the three questions a senior audience will ask and the two-sentence answer to each before you present.
Present to the C-suite or board using your restructured deck with implications first, and time how quickly they ask their anticipated questions.

topics.title: Handling Tough Questions Gracefully
topics.description: Prepare for hostile, off-topic, and impossibly broad questions by learning the PREP framework, bridging techniques, and how to say "I don't know" without losing credibility.

steps.d: For an upcoming meeting with skeptics or critics, write down the five questions or objections you're most worried about.
For each tough question, write your answer as: Point (your position), Reason (why), Example (proof), Point (restate your position).
For questions that go outside your prep, rehearse phrases like "That's an important point—here's what matters for today's decision" to redirect back on message.
Practice the phrase "I don't know that offhand, and I'll find out and follow up by Tuesday" in front of a mirror without hedging or over-explaining.

steps.t: Run a mock Q and A
steps.d: Have a colleague ask your five toughest questions back-to-back while you practice PREP answers and bridging, then ask if your answers held up.

topics.title: Crisis and High-Pressure Communication
topics.description: Communicate credibly when things go wrong — projecting calm under pressure, sticking to the facts, and rebuilding trust with stakeholders after a setback.

steps.d: Write down a plausible crisis or setback for your team or company and outline what you'd need to communicate in the first 24 hours.

steps.t: Build a fact vs. speculation list
steps.d: For your crisis scenario, write down what you know for certain and what you're still figuring out, and practice communicating only the known facts.
Write a 3-4 sentence statement you could give in the first hours of crisis that's honest but buys you time: facts plus "we're investigating" or "more to come."
Record yourself delivering your holding statement and your initial updates—practice a measured pace and steady tone to project confidence.
After using crisis communication in a real situation, write down what worked and what you'd change, identifying one improvement for next time.

topics.title: Executive Memo Writing
topics.description: Write the memo that gets acted on: one-page format, clear headline, supporting bullets, and a crisp ask — written for someone who will read it between meetings.

steps.d: Create a memo template with section headings: TO/FROM/DATE, headline (main point), background (context), recommendation (what you want them to do), supporting points (grouped bullets).
Draft a one-page memo on a real decision or issue at work, leading with your recommendation and keeping supporting points to four bullets.
Read your memo aloud—it should take 2-3 minutes to read; if it takes longer, cut half the words.

steps.t: Add a clear call to action
steps.d: Revise your memo to end with a specific ask: approve by Thursday, provide feedback by end of day, or schedule a follow-up meeting.
Send the memo to your intended reader and ask if they understand what you're recommending and what you're asking them to do.

topics.title: Email Communication at Senior Levels
topics.description: Apply military-precision email techniques — action-required subject lines, bottom-line-up-front structure, and micro-formatting — to emails that get fast decisions.

steps.d: Review three emails you sent this week and mark the first sentence—does it state the action needed, or do you bury it?

steps.t: Write subject lines that command action
steps.d: Take three routine emails and rewrite their subject lines to include action: "Decision needed by Friday: Team budget allocation" instead of "Budget discussion."

steps.t: Apply BLUFF structure to one email
steps.d: Draft an email using Bottom Line Up Front: open with your request or conclusion, then provide supporting details only if needed.
Take a longer email and reformat it with numbered points (1. What I need, 2. By when, 3. Next steps) so a busy reader gets it in 30 seconds.
Send three emails using action-first structure and track how much faster you get responses compared to your previous approach.

topics.title: Concise Writing Under Pressure
topics.description: Develop the editing instinct that separates executive writers from the rest — cut word count by 30%, remove hedging language, and write first drafts that don't bury the point.

steps.t: Count words in your first draft
steps.d: Write a draft memo or email on a real topic and count the total words.
Rewrite the same memo removing all hedging, qualifiers, and extra examples until it's 30% shorter.
Scan your draft and eliminate phrases like "I think," "sort of," "kind of," "might be," and "in my opinion"—state facts instead.
Replace "is able to" with "can," "is in a position to" with "will," and other verbose constructions.
Read your condensed version out loud and confirm every sentence still makes sense and the main point is even sharper.
